passages.happening:
‘Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled by your iniquity’ (verse 1). Hosea tells the people to bring words with them and return. He gives them the words to say: ‘Take away all our iniquity and receive us graciously, that we may present the fruit of our lips’ (verse 2).

The prayer goes on. Assyria will not save them, and they will not ride on horses. They will never again call the work of their own hands their gods. ‘For in You the fatherless find compassion’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is not tied to an event that can be dated, and scholars differ on whether it was spoken before Samaria's fall as a last appeal, or kept afterward as a word of hope for survivors and for Judah. Its content fits Hosea's world closely. Assyria was the power Israel had tried to buy off, and horses stood for military strength and for alliances with Egypt, famous for its chariot horses. Giving up both meant giving up the whole plan by which Israel's last kings had tried to survive.

Hosea does not only call the people back. He puts a prayer in their mouths, beginning with a request for forgiveness and ending with a confession of trust. Its offering is words. The standard Hebrew text reads something like bulls of the lips, words of praise offered in place of sacrificial bulls, while the ancient Greek translation reads fruit of the lips, as the BSB does in its own wording. Either way, the people bring confession and praise.

The last line draws on the law's care for orphans, who had no one to protect them. Israel, having lost its false protectors, comes to God as an orphan. The word return, shuv, runs through the chapter and ties it together.
passages.later: Isaiah warned Judah in the same way against those who ‘rely on horses’ (Isaiah 31:1). A psalm calls God ‘A father of the fatherless’ (Psalm 68:5). The Letter to the Hebrews calls believers to offer God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess his name, using the phrase this verse has in its Greek form (Hebrews 13:15).
passages.asks: Hosea gave Israel words to pray when it had none of its own. Ask what your own version of this prayer would include. And ask what you would need to name and give up, as Israel gave up Assyria and horses and idols, to come back to God with your whole heart.

passages.happening:
God answers the prayer. ‘I will heal their apostasy; I will freely love them, for My anger has turned away from them’ (verse 4).

‘I will be like the dew to Israel; he will blossom like the lily and take root like the cedars of Lebanon’ (verse 5). His shoots will spread, his beauty will be like the olive tree and his fragrance like Lebanon (verse 6). People will dwell again in his shade, grow grain and blossom like the vine (verse 7). God asks what Ephraim has to do with idols anymore. He is the one who answers and watches over him. ‘I am like a flourishing cypress; your fruit comes from Me’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Dew mattered greatly in a land where rain fell only in the winter months. Through the long dry summer, heavy night dew off the sea kept crops and vines alive. Earlier Hosea compared Israel's fickle love to dew that vanishes in the morning (6:4; 13:3). Now God himself will be the dew that keeps Israel alive.

Lebanon, named three times, was the mountain range to the north, famous for its tall cedars, its fragrant forests and its wines. To people in the hot, dry hill country it meant height, permanence and plenty. The lily, the olive, the grain and the vine are pictures of a land in flower, the opposite of the ruin threatened in chapter 2.

God speaks in the first person through a stream of pictures from nature, and ends by calling himself a flourishing cypress, the only place in the Old Testament where God compares himself to a tree. Israel had looked for fruitfulness from Baal. Its fruit comes from the LORD.
passages.later: The fruitless vine and the dry land of Hosea 2 are reversed here (Hosea 2:12). A psalm pictures the righteous in the same way, flourishing ‘like a cedar in Lebanon’ (Psalm 92:12).
passages.asks: God says he will love them freely, not because they have earned it. Ask whether you believe God's love toward you is free. And God says he will be like the dew, quiet and daily. Ask where you have missed his quiet care while waiting for something dramatic.

passages.happening: The book closes with a word to anyone who reads it. ‘Whoever is wise, let him understand these things; whoever is discerning, let him know them. For the ways of the LORD are right, and the righteous walk in them but the rebellious stumble in them’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This last verse is a short epilogue in the style of the wisdom books, like the sayings of Proverbs. It speaks not to Hosea's first hearers in Samaria but to every later reader of the whole book. The book was kept and copied in Judah after the north fell, and this verse hands it on.

It calls the reader to choose. The same ways of the LORD are a road for the righteous and a stumbling block for the rebellious. The word stumble picks up the first verse of the chapter, where Israel has stumbled by its iniquity. A reader who has heard the whole of Hosea, the marriage and the lawsuit, the calf and the whirlwind, the Father and the lion, is asked to understand it and to walk in it.
passages.later: The wisdom books speak the same way: ‘The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom’ (Proverbs 9:10). The psalms open with the same two ways, of the righteous and the wicked (Psalm 1:6).
passages.asks: The last verse asks the reader to understand and to walk. Ask what you will take from Hosea into your own life. And ask whether the ways of the LORD have been a road for you, or a place where you keep stumbling.
